# Transcaval Access for Structural Heart Interventions: A Narrative Review

## Introduction
Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) has revolutionized the treatment of severe, symptomatic aortic stenosis. While the transfemoral approach remains the clinical gold standard, severe peripheral artery disease (PAD), small vessel diameters, excessive calcification, and extreme tortuosity preclude safe transfemoral delivery in approximately 10% to 15% of candidates [1,2]. Historically, such patients were routed to surgical alternative access pathways—including transapical, transaortic, and subclavian/axillary approaches—which carry significant surgical morbidity, elevated mortality rates, and prolonged recovery periods [3,4]. In response to these limitations, percutaneous caval-aortic (transcaval) access was introduced as a novel, fully percutaneous alternative for large-bore structural heart interventions [5].

## Anatomy and Physiology of Caval-Aortic Access
The transcaval technique involves traversing the wall of the inferior vena cava (IVC) into the adjacent abdominal aorta [6]. While creating a direct aortocaval fistula may intuitively seem hazardous, the approach is supported by unique retroperitoneal anatomical and physiological principles [7]. In the infrarenal space, the abdominal aorta and IVC run parallel and are separated by a minimal amount of soft tissue [8,9]. Furthermore, the retroperitoneal space acts as a closed, high-pressure chamber. When the communication tract is closed or occupied by a sheath, retroperitoneal pressure exceeds venous pressure, preventing free retroperitoneal extravasation and redirecting any residual bleeding into the low-pressure venous system [10,11].

## Pre-Procedural Planning and Patient Selection
Meticulous pre-procedural planning is the cornerstone of a successful transcaval procedure. Multi-detector computed tomography (MDCT) is indispensable for identifying an eligible "crossing window" [12]. Ideally, this window is located in the infrarenal aorta, free of severe calcification, thrombus, or major side branches (such as the renal, lumbar, or mesenteric arteries) at the site of puncture, and directly adjacent to an accessible, non-calcified segment of the IVC [13]. Precise trajectory measurement and coordinate mapping are completed to guide fluoroscopy and electrosurgical crossing [14].

## Procedural Technique
The procedure is performed under fluoroscopic guidance, typically using a co-axial catheter system introduced through the femoral vein [15]. A standard coronary guidewire is energized with electrosurgery (cautery) to cross from the IVC into the aorta under orthogonal fluoroscopic views [16]. Once crossing is achieved, the wire is advanced into the aorta and captured using an endovascular snare introduced via a secondary, small-bore transfemoral arterial access [17]. A stiff guidewire is then positioned, allowing a large-bore delivery sheath to be advanced from the femoral vein, across the IVC-aorta tract, and up the abdominal aorta to perform the primary structural intervention (e.g., TAVR) [18,19]. After completion of the intervention, the aortocaval tract must be securely closed. This is accomplished using an off-label nitinol cardiac occluder, most commonly an Amplatzer Duct Occluder (ADO), deployed across the aortic and venous walls under fluoroscopic and angiographic monitoring [20,21].

## Clinical Outcomes and Registry Data
Initial clinical registries demonstrated the high feasibility and efficacy of this technique [22,23]. The landmark National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) prospective transcaval registry confirmed a procedural success rate of over 98%, with low rates of major vascular complications and 30-day mortality despite high-risk baseline profiles [5,24]. Long-term data, including 1-year follow-up from the NHLBI registry, have demonstrated excellent closure durability, high rates of fistula occlusion (exceeding 90%), and a low incidence of late-onset aortic complications or symptomatic shunts [25].

## Broader Applications and Future Directions
While initially developed for TAVR, the utility of transcaval access has expanded to other large-bore vascular and structural interventions. These include endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR) [26], thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) [27], and transcatheter mitral valve replacement (TMVR) [28]. Despite the introduction of lower-profile delivery sheaths that have decreased the overall cohort of patients requiring alternative access, transcaval access remains a critical bailout strategy [29]. Comparative analyses indicate that transcaval access is associated with shorter hospital stays and lower 30-day mortality compared to traditional surgical alternative routes [30].

## Conclusion
Transcaval access is a safe, effective, and fully percutaneous alternative to surgical cutdown for patients requiring large-bore structural heart interventions. Continued refinements in technique, improved operator experience, and the development of dedicated, purpose-built closure devices are expected to further solidify its role in the modern interventional armamentarium.
